title: The Fibonacci Pair Is the Unique Euclidean Worst Case
description: Strengthens Lamé sharpness from existence to uniqueness: any pair (a, b) with 0 < b < a taking n steps and attaining the minimal larger input a = fib(n+2) is forced to have b = fib(n+1) exactly. Answers open question OQ-05 of the parent gcd-algorithm-oq-01, proving the Fibonacci pair is the single extremal pair on the a-side, self-contained and axiom-free.

meta.author: Lean Genius
meta.assumptions: None. Fully machine-verified from the foundational axioms (propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound); #print axioms confirms all five headline theorems use no others. Small Fibonacci values are discharged by decide (kernel reduction), NOT native_decide, so Lean.ofReduceBool is not used. The entry is self-contained: it re-derives its own step counter and both Lamé bounds rather than importing them.
originalContributions: worst_case_forces_fib: the forcing/uniqueness result — if 0 < b < a takes n ≥ 1 steps and a = fib(n+2), then b is forced to the exact value fib(n+1). This is the new content: sharpness (an extremal pair exists) upgraded to uniqueness (it is the only one on the a-side).
worst_case_iff: full characterisation — for n ≥ 1 the pairs (a, b) with 0 < b < a, n steps, and a = fib(n+2) are precisely the singleton {(fib(n+2), fib(n+1))}.
worst_case_pair_unique: packaged statement a = fib(n+2) ∧ b = fib(n+1) under the extremal hypotheses.

lame_pair_bound: a single strong-induction engine returning BOTH fib(n+1) ≤ b and, one level down, fib n ≤ a % b — the two-sided bound that drives the forcing via the squeeze a = fib n + fib(n+1), a % b = a − b, fib n ≤ a % b.
steps_a_lower_bound / steps_sum_lower_bound: the a-side Lamé bound fib(n+2) ≤ a and the size bound fib(n+3) ≤ a + b, re-derived self-contained.

conclusion.summary: Proves the Fibonacci pair is the UNIQUE Euclidean worst case on the larger input. Where the sibling gcd-algorithm-oq-01-oq-03-oq-01 shows the Fibonacci pairs are extremal (fib(n+2) ≤ a, fib(n+1) ≤ b, both attained), this entry shows attaining the a-bound a = fib(n+2) forces b = fib(n+1) exactly — no other second input in the window [fib(n+1), fib(n+2)) reaches n steps against a = fib(n+2). 15 theorems, 1 definition, 0 axioms, 0 sorries, 313 lines.
conclusion.implications: The forcing is genuinely one-directional, which the entry documents with a concrete witness: attaining the b-bound does NOT force the Fibonacci pair — (a, b) = (5, 2) at n = 2 has b = fib 3 = 2 yet a = 5 ≠ fib 4 = 3. The larger input is the rigid coordinate: once a hits its minimum fib(n+2) = fib n + fib(n+1), the interval fib(n+1) ≤ b < a is squeezed by the one-level-down remainder bound fib n ≤ a % b, collapsing b to fib(n+1). This pins the entire extremal set on the a-side to a single point and completes the uniqueness half of Lamé's 1844 analysis, historically the first worst-case complexity analysis of an algorithm.
openQuestions: Characterise the full a-fibre without fixing a: for arbitrary a, describe exactly which b in [1, a) maximise euclidSteps a b, and count them — the (5, 2) witness shows this count exceeds one when a is not itself Fibonacci.

Prove the analogous uniqueness for the subtractive (slow) GCD or the binary (Stein) GCD, where the tight family (1, 2^n − 1) is known from binary-gcd-oq-01-oq-04 but its extremal uniqueness is unformalized.

crossReferences.description: Parent entry on Euclidean worst/average-case complexity; its open question OQ-05 asks for equality in Lamé's bound to force (a, b) = (fib(n+2), fib(n+1)), which this entry proves on the a-side.
Sibling proving Lamé sharpness — Fibonacci pairs realize n steps and are minimal (both bounds attained). This entry adds the uniqueness/forcing direction that sharpness alone does not give.
The analogous tight worst-case family (1, 2^n − 1) for the binary GCD, a structural contrast whose extremal uniqueness remains open.

sections.title: Module Overview and References
sections.summary: Module docstring stating the uniqueness open question OQ-05: any Euclidean pair (a,b) with 0<b<a taking n division steps satisfies fib(n+2)≤a and fib(n+1)≤b, with equality forcing (a,b)=(fib(n+2),fib(n+1)). Explains that the forcing is one-directional (the larger input a is the rigid one) and that the whole entry runs off the single strong-induction bound lame_pair_bound, staying axiom-free by discharging small Fibonacci values with kernel `decide` (no Lean.ofReduceBool).
sections.mathContext: Lamé's 1844 theorem: a pair requiring $n$ steps has $a\ge F_{n+2}$, $b\ge F_{n+1}$. Attaining the $b$-bound does not force the Fibonacci pair (e.g. $n=2$, $b=F_3=2$, $a=5$ also takes 2 steps), but attaining $a=F_{n+2}$ squeezes $b$ into $[F_{n+1},F_{n+2})$ and the remainder bound $F_n\le a\bmod b$ collapses it to $F_{n+1}$.

sections.title: Self-Contained Step Counter and Basic Lemmas
sections.summary: Defines the well-founded step counter `euclideanSteps a b` (0 when b=0, else euclideanSteps b (a%b)+1) with termination on b, re-derived here so the entry stands alone. Provides `euclideanSteps_zero`, the positive-argument unfolding `euclideanSteps_pos_eq`, the lower bound `euclideanSteps_ge_one`, the zero characterisation `euclideanSteps_eq_zero_iff`, and the Fibonacci mod identity `fib_mod_fib`: fib(n+2) % fib(n+1) = fib n for n≥2.
sections.mathContext: The counter mirrors the Euclidean recursion $\gcd(a,b)=\gcd(b,a\bmod b)$. The key arithmetic fact $F_{n+2}\bmod F_{n+1}=F_n$ follows from $F_{n+2}=F_n+F_{n+1}$ with $0\le F_n<F_{n+1}$, so one Euclidean step sends the pair $(F_{n+2},F_{n+1})$ to $(F_{n+1},F_n)$.

sections.title: The Two-Sided Lamé Bound (Strong Induction)
sections.summary: The proof engine `lame_pair_bound`: by strong induction on the step count n, if euclideanSteps a b = n and b>0 then fib(n+1)≤b, and moreover fib n ≤ a%b once n≥2. The base cases n=0,1 are handled by unfolding; the inductive step peels one division, applies the hypothesis to (b, a%b), and lifts via the Fibonacci recurrence. `lame_b_lower_bound` extracts the b-side as a standalone corollary.
sections.mathContext: Returning both $F_{n+1}\le b$ and $F_n\le a\bmod b$ from one induction is what makes the later forcing possible: the remainder bound one level down is exactly the extra rigidity needed to pin $b$.

sections.title: The Fibonacci Pair Achieves n Steps
sections.summary: `euclideanSteps_fib`: consecutive Fibonacci numbers realise the worst case, euclideanSteps (fib(n+2)) (fib(n+1)) = n for n≥1. Induction from the base euclideanSteps (fib 3) (fib 2) = euclideanSteps 2 1 = 1, using the reduction fib(n+3) % fib(n+2) = fib(n+1) to drop the count by one each step.
sections.mathContext: This is the existence (achievability) half of Lamé sharpness; combined with the lower bound it shows the Fibonacci pair is extremal, and combined with the forcing result it shows it is the *unique* extremal pair.

sections.title: The a-Side Bound
sections.summary: `steps_a_lower_bound`: if (a,b) takes n≥1 steps with 0<b<a then fib(n+2)≤a. For n=1 the remainder vanishes so b∣a with a>b gives a≥2b; for n≥2 the remainder bound fib n ≤ a%b combines with fib(n+1)≤b through a = b·(a/b) + a%b ≥ b + a%b and the recurrence fib(n+2)=fib n + fib(n+1).
sections.mathContext: The $a$-side is the bound Lamé's original argument targets; it is the constraint that, once tight, forces the whole pair.

sections.title: The Forcing / Uniqueness Result
sections.summary: The heart of the entry. `worst_case_forces_fib`: a pair with 0<b<a taking n≥1 steps and attaining a=fib(n+2) has b forced to exactly fib(n+1). `worst_case_pair_unique` packages the pair equality, and `worst_case_iff` gives the full characterisation: for n≥1 the pairs with 0<b<a, n steps, and a=fib(n+2) are precisely {(fib(n+2),fib(n+1))}. The forcing uses a%b = a-b (valid since a<2b) together with fib n ≤ a%b.
sections.mathContext: Uniqueness upgrades Lamé from an inequality to an equality-with-rigidity statement: the extremal input is not just bounded but pinned. The identity $a\bmod b=a-b$ holds because $F_{n+1}\le b$ and $a=F_{n+2}<2F_{n+1}$.

sections.title: Size Bound
sections.summary: `steps_sum_lower_bound`: any pair taking n≥1 steps with 0<b<a has a+b ≥ fib(n+3), with equality for the Fibonacci pair since fib(n+2)+fib(n+1)=fib(n+3). Follows by adding the a-side and b-side bounds and applying the Fibonacci recurrence.
sections.mathContext: The sum bound is the natural 'total size' formulation of Lamé's theorem, matching the classical statement that inputs below a size threshold force at most logarithmically many steps.

sections.title: Numerical Sanity Checks
sections.summary: Kernel-`decide` verifications that Fibonacci values are concrete: worst_pair_four (fib 6, fib 5)=(8,5) and sum_seven fib6+fib5=13=fib7, plus `#print axioms` confirmations that the main theorems depend only on the standard foundational axioms (no Lean.ofReduceBool), keeping the entry axiom-free.

overview.historicalContext: Lamé's theorem (1844) is often cited as the first complexity analysis of an algorithm: it bounds the number of division steps of the Euclidean algorithm and identifies consecutive Fibonacci numbers as the extremal inputs. The standard modern statement is two-sided — an upper bound (~5 steps per decimal digit via log_φ) and a sharpness claim (Fibonacci pairs attain it). Sharpness says an extremal pair EXISTS; it does not by itself say the extremal pair is UNIQUE. This entry settles the uniqueness question the parent poses.
overview.problemStatement: Show that any pair (a, b) with 0 < b < a requiring n ≥ 1 Euclidean division steps satisfies a ≥ fib(n+2) and b ≥ fib(n+1), and that equality in the a-bound forces the pair to be exactly (fib(n+2), fib(n+1)). Equivalently, for n ≥ 1 the set of pairs with 0 < b < a, n steps, and a = fib(n+2) is precisely the singleton {(fib(n+2), fib(n+1))}.
overview.proofStrategy: Everything runs off one strong-induction lemma, lame_pair_bound, which returns simultaneously fib(n+1) ≤ b and, one level down, fib n ≤ a % b. Given the extremal hypothesis a = fib(n+2) = fib n + fib(n+1) with fib(n+1) ≤ b < a, one has a < 2b, hence a % b = a − b; combined with fib n ≤ a % b this yields b ≤ fib(n+1), and with the lower bound b = fib(n+1) exactly. The reverse inclusion (the Fibonacci pair really takes n steps and satisfies the constraints) uses euclideanSteps_fib, proved by induction from the base (fib 3, fib 2) = (2, 1) via the Fibonacci mod identity fib(n+2) % fib(n+1) = fib n. Small Fibonacci values are closed by decide, keeping the entry axiom-free.
keyInsights: Uniqueness is strictly stronger than sharpness: sharpness gives an extremal pair; this entry shows it is the ONLY extremal pair on the a-side, collapsing the whole fibre a = fib(n+2) to a single b.

The forcing is one-directional. Attaining the a-bound rigidly fixes b, but attaining the b-bound does not fix a — witness (a, b) = (5, 2) at n = 2, where b = fib 3 = 2 yet a = 5 ≠ fib 4. The larger input is the rigid coordinate.

A single two-sided induction lemma does all the work: lame_pair_bound returns fib(n+1) ≤ b together with the one-level-down remainder bound fib n ≤ a % b, which is exactly the squeeze needed to trap b.
The collapse is pure linear arithmetic once the pieces are in place: a = fib n + fib(n+1), a % b = a − b (because a < 2b), and fib n ≤ a % b force b ≤ fib(n+1), meeting the lower bound with equality.
The account is deliberately self-contained: it re-derives its own euclideanSteps counter and both Lamé bounds rather than importing them, so the uniqueness argument can be read end to end.
